title: Improving Conditional Modeling via Inter-Class Likelihood-Ratio Maximization and Unifying Classifier-Free Guidance with Alignment Objectives
claim: A reference model's class-conditional distributions overlap and blur class identity; fine-tuning separates them so samples show distinct class features.
layout: 2 stacked panels, top-to-bottom, central fine-tune arrow, sample images flanking density curves
description: Two vertically stacked panels, (a) and (b), each showing a 1-D density sketch with two modes labeled c1 and c2. A gray curve for p_data is overlaid with a colored curve. In (a), the blue p_ref curve is flat and broad, spilling into the valley between the modes. Above the modes are blue-bordered sample images: messy, ambiguous burgers on the left and blurry warthogs on the right. A gradient arrow labeled 'MCLR Finetune' points down to (b). There, the purple p_MCLR curve hugs the gray p_data modes more tightly, with a deeper valley between them. The purple-bordered samples are clean, distinct burgers and warthogs. Captions under each panel read 'not sufficiently separated' and 'more separated'. The eye goes first to the images and the two-peaked curves.
caption: Conceptual Illustration of MCLR. (a) Samples generated from two classes using the same initial noises exhibit high visual similarity despite different conditioning labels, indicating insufficient separation of the learned conditional distributions. (b) MCLR mitigates this issue by encouraging inter-class separation, resulting in generations with more distinct class-specific features.
abstract: Diffusion models achieve strong generative performance but often rely on classifier-free guidance (CFG), an inference-time intervention that modifies the sampling trajectory. Since standard denoising score matching (DSM) should recover the target distribution when the score is learned accurately, the practical necessity of CFG suggests deficiencies in learned conditional scores. We identify weak inter-class separation as one such limitation: samples generated from the same noise under different labels can retain similar class-agnostic structure. To address this deficiency, we introduce MCLR, a principled fine-tuning objective that explicitly maximizes inter-class likelihood-ratios, thereby strengthening class-specific structures under standard sampling. Across diverse models and datasets, MCLR substantially improves guidance-free conditional generation and narrows the gap to CFG. Theoretically, we prove that the CFG-guided score is the unique minimizer of a sample-adaptively weighted, ELBO-approximated MCLR objective, interpreting CFG as an implicit inference-time contrastive alignment procedure. We further compare MCLR with related contrastive objectives, including DPO, CCA, and CFM, clarifying their connections and key differences in an otherwise fragmented literature.
